author: Augustine of Hippo
occasion: Paulinus wrote to ask whether it benefits a person after death to be buried near the memorial shrine of a saint. The question was prompted by a widow Flora's request for her deceased son to be buried in the basilica of the confessor Felix; Paulinus had already reported that the body of the faithful young man Cynegius, a different person, had been placed there.
argument: Augustine argues that burial location does not directly help or harm the dead, since the dead cannot sense what happens to their bodies. What benefits the dead is the living's prayerful remembrance, which can be increased when a body is buried at a holy memorial. The dead do not know what the living do while it is happening, but may learn afterwards from those who die and come to them, or from angels, or by divine revelation; and God may specially send them to the living. Therefore Christians should care for the dead out of human affection and faith in the resurrection, but should place their hope in prayers and the church's commemoration, not in the place of burial.

outline.move: Augustine states Paulinus's question and resolves the apparent conflict with Paul's statement that each will be judged for what was done in the body.
He argues from Scripture and reason that lack of burial does not harm the dead, while burial is still a proper act of piety toward the body.
He explains that burial at a martyr's memorial helps the dead only insofar as it stirs the living to commend them in prayer.

He discusses examples of unburied martyrs (8), the human affection for burial and the scriptural example of the prophet denied burial (9), the martyrs' victory over this affection (10), and the 'miserable compassion' of those who bury the dead (11).
He examines visions of the dead in dreams and waking visions, arguing these are usually images produced by angelic operation, not the dead themselves appearing.

Section 16 argues the dead do not know living affairs; section 17 addresses the objection about the rich man in the parable; section 18 admits the dead may learn from those who die or from angels; section 19 addresses how martyrs help if the dead do not know living affairs.
He confesses uncertainty about how martyrs help the living, whether by their own presence or through angels, and gives examples of such divine operations.
He concludes with practical counsel: prayers, the altar, and alms benefit the dead who merited such help in life, and burial at a martyr's memorial helps by increasing the supplication of the living.

cast.name: Paulinus
cast.who: Bishop of Nola, the addressee of the letter.

cast.name: Flora
cast.who: A religious widow who asked Paulinus about burial for her deceased son.

cast.name: Cynegius
cast.who: A faithful young man whose body was already placed in the basilica of Felix; he is distinct from the widow Flora's son, though both were buried in the same region.

cast.name: Felix
cast.who: A confessor (not explicitly called martyr in the text) venerated at Nola, whose basilica is mentioned.

cast.name: Curma
cast.who: A poor town councillor from Tullium near Hippo who had a vision while near death.

cast.name: Eulogius
cast.who: A rhetorician of Carthage and former student of Augustine, who dreamed Augustine explained a passage of Cicero.

cast.name: John
cast.who: A monk and prophet consulted by the emperor Theodosius the Elder about a civil war.

cast.name: Ambrose
cast.who: Bishop of Milan, still living when demons at the shrines of Protasius and Gervasius begged him for mercy.

cast.name: Candidianus
cast.who: A brother and fellow presbyter who carried the letter to Paulinus.

voices.speaker: Paulinus (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Augustine reports Paulinus's view with 'dicis' and indirect statement

voices.speaker: Scripture (Paul, Psalms, prophets, Gospel)
voices.how_marked: Introduced with 'dicit apostolus', 'dicitur in psalmo', 'haec dicit dominus', etc.

voices.speaker: Virgil (paraphrased, not directly quoted with quotation marks)
voices.how_marked: Introduced with 'sicut apud Maronem legitur'; Augustine gives a Latin prose paraphrase of Aeneid 6.325-330, not a direct verse quotation

voices.speaker: The rich man in the parable
voices.how_marked: Introduced as the rich man speaking to Abraham

voices.speaker: John the monk
voices.how_marked: Direct speech introduced with 'inquit'; reported speech within Augustine's narrative, not a quotation Augustine heard directly

key_terms.sense: A shrine or monument at the burial place of a martyr or saint, intended to keep the dead in remembrance
Burial or the act and manner of burying the dead
Commending the dead to God in prayer, especially at the altar
Prayer of entreaty offered for the dead
Those who died confessing Christ and are venerated as saints
The natural human feeling or disposition, especially love for one's own flesh and for the dead
The soul or spirit of a deceased person, as distinct from the body
The underworld or place of the dead, sometimes in a pagan or poetic sense
The eucharistic offering made at the altar, also offered for the dead
Alms or charitable gifts, which can benefit the dead when offered for them
The baptized, those born again in Christ, for whom the church prays
A vision or dream-appearance, often of the dead to the living
A likeness or image of a person seen in a dream or vision, not the person himself
The advocacy or intercession of martyrs on behalf of the dead

scripture: Augustine uses Old Latin versions of Scripture, generally following the Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering. He cites 'the books of the Machabees' (Maccabees), 'the books of the Kingdoms' (1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings), 'Ecclesiasticus' (Sirach), and the Psalms according to the Septuagint numbering. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names: 1-2 Maccabees, 1-2 Samuel, 1-2 Kings, Sirach, and the Hebrew Psalm numbering where it differs from the Septuagint.
uncertain: The precise date of composition is not stated in the text; c. 421 is a scholarly estimate.
Whether the 'John the monk' consulted by Theodosius is the same as John of Lycopolis is not stated in the text.
The exact identity of the 'bishop' demons confessed at Milan is given as Ambrose, but the text does not specify the date of this event.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paulinus had already reported that the body of the faithful young man Cynegius, a different person, had been placed there
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: idque etiam nuntians de cadauere fidelis iuuenis Cynegii, quod materno et pio affectu desiderauit, esse conpletum, ut scilicet in beatissimi Felicis confessoris basilica poneretur
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cynegius was the son of the widow Flora; the text states that Flora 'desiderauit' (desired/wished) this for him with maternal and pious affection, and that Paulinus reported it had been accomplished. The brief incorrectly makes Cynegius a separate person from Flora's son.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cynegius... is distinct from the widow Flora's son, though both were buried in the same region
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: utrum prosit cuique post mortem, quod corpus eius apud sancti alicuius memoriam sepelitur. hoc enim abs te uidua memorata petiuerat pro defuncto in eis partibus suo filio et rescripseras consolans eam: idque etiam nuntians de cadauere fidelis iuuenis Cynegii, quod materno et pio affectu desiderauit, esse conpletum
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cynegius IS Flora's son. The text explicitly says Flora 'petiuerat pro defuncto... suo filio' (asked for her deceased son) and then refers to 'fidelis iuuenis Cynegii, quod materno et pio affectu desiderauit' (the faithful young man Cynegius, which she desired with maternal and pious affection). The 'quod' refers back to the son.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Felix... A confessor (not explicitly called martyr in the text)
_unresolved_facts.fix: Felix is explicitly called 'confessoris' (confessor), not martyr, in the text. The brief is correct but should note that Augustine later discusses martyrs generally and Felix's shrine specifically without calling Felix a martyr.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Virgil (paraphrased, not directly quoted with quotation marks)... Augustine gives a Latin prose paraphrase of Aeneid 6.325-330
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: nec ripas datur horrendas et rauca fluenta transportare prius, quam sedibus ossa quierunt
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief's citation of Aeneid 6.325-330 is unsupported by the text itself; the text does not identify the specific lines. The brief should simply note Augustine paraphrases Virgil without specifying lines, or verify the citation against a modern edition.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Section 16 argues the dead do not know living affairs; section 17 addresses the objection about the rich man in the parable; section 18 admits the dead may learn from those who die or from angels
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Dixerit aliquis: si nulla est mortuis cura de uiuis, quomodo ille diues...
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 17 begins with an objection about the rich man, but section 16 already anticipates this with 'quomodo ergo uident tumulos suos aut corpora sua' and the discussion of Isaiah and Josiah. The outline oversimplifies: section 16 argues the dead do not know living affairs AND anticipates objections; section 17 specifically addresses the rich man parable; section 18 admits the dead may learn after the fact.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['8', '9', '10', '11']... He discusses examples of unburied martyrs (8), the human affection for burial and the scriptural example of the prophet denied burial (9), the martyrs' victory over this affection (10), and the 'miserable compassion' of those who bury the dead (11)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Secundum istam quam dixi miseram conpassionem laudantur illi et a rege Dauid benedicuntur, qui Saulis et Ionathae ossibus aridis sepulturae misericordiam praestiterunt
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 11 discusses David blessing those who buried Saul and Jonathan, but this is not 'those who bury the dead' generally—it's specifically about Saul and Jonathan, who were enemies of David. The 'miserable compassion' applies to those who could not bury the martyrs in section 10, not to those who buried Saul and Jonathan in 11. The outline conflates the two groups.

_unresolved_facts.claim: John... A monk and prophet consulted by the emperor Theodosius the Elder about a civil war
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Talem fuisse credendum est illum Iohannem monachum, quem de belli ciuilis euentu maior Theodosius consuluit imperator: habebat quippe etiam prophetiam
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text calls him 'maior Theodosius' (the elder Theodosius), not 'Theodosius the Elder'—the brief's rendering is acceptable but should note the Latin form. More importantly, the brief's uncertainty note correctly states 'Whether the 'John the monk' consulted by Theodosius is the same as John of Lycopolis is not stated in the text'—but the main cast entry presents this identification as certain.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Ambrose... still living when demons at the shrines of Protasius and Gervasius begged him for mercy
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: adhuc uiuum daemones episcopum confitebantur Ambrosium atque ut sibi parceret obsecrabant illo aliud agente atque hoc cum ageretur omnino nesciente
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says Ambrose was 'adhuc uiuum' (still living) and 'illo aliud agente atque hoc cum ageretur omnino nesciente' (doing something else and completely unaware this was happening). The brief's 'begged him for mercy' is slightly off—'ut sibi parceret' means 'that he spare them,' i.e., stop tormenting them or let them go.
